questions.question: A client with prior abdominal surgery has cramping pain, distension, vomiting, and little flatus. What should the RN suspect?
choices: Possible mechanical bowel obstruction requiring prompt assessment
Uncomplicated GERD based on vomiting alone
Normal bowel function because some stool might still pass
A diagnosis that bowel sounds alone can exclude
questions.explanation: Adhesions after surgery can cause obstruction. Pain, distension, emesis, and altered passage of stool or gas warrant prompt evaluation; partial obstruction may still allow some stool.

questions.question: A client being observed for bowel obstruction develops constant severe pain, abdominal rigidity, fever, and tachycardia. What is the priority concern?
choices: Strangulation, ischemia, or perforation requiring urgent surgical reassessment
Expected improvement from decompression
Mild dietary intolerance only
A harmless change that can wait until morning rounds
questions.explanation: New continuous pain and peritoneal or systemic signs can indicate bowel ischemia or perforation. A prior plan for conservative care must be reconsidered immediately.

questions.question: Which order set is most consistent with initial nonoperative management of an uncomplicated adhesive small-bowel obstruction?
choices: NPO, prescribed IV fluids and electrolyte correction, NG decompression when ordered, and serial reassessment
Unrestricted oral meals and laxatives without surgical review
No intake-output monitoring if the client is alert
Automatic discharge after one episode of vomiting
questions.explanation: For a stable client without peritonitis or ischemia, conservative management commonly includes bowel rest, decompression, fluid and electrolyte support, and frequent reassessment.

questions.question: Which description best distinguishes Crohn disease from ulcerative colitis?
choices: Crohn disease can involve any GI segment and the full bowel wall; UC is a continuous colonic mucosal disease beginning at the rectum
UC always produces fistulas through the entire bowel wall while Crohn disease never does
Both conditions are diagnosed from stool color alone
Crohn disease affects only the rectum
questions.explanation: Crohn disease may be transmural and discontinuous across the GI tract, increasing stricture and fistula risk; UC typically has continuous mucosal colonic inflammation.

questions.question: A hospitalized client with severe UC has increasing abdominal distension, fever, tachycardia, and worsening pain. What complication needs urgent evaluation?
choices: Toxic megacolon with possible perforation or sepsis
Routine remission without complications
Simple constipation that needs an unsupervised laxative
Expected effect of every IBD medicine
questions.explanation: Severe colitis plus systemic toxicity and progressive distension is concerning for toxic megacolon; prompt specialist assessment and monitoring are essential.

questions.question: An immunocompetent client has mild imaging-confirmed uncomplicated diverticulitis. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Antibiotics may be selected rather than automatic for every mild uncomplicated case, based on the full clinical assessment
Every episode requires emergency surgery
A normal diet always treats perforation
No follow-up is needed if pain improves
questions.explanation: AGA guidance supports selective rather than routine antibiotics in immunocompetent mild uncomplicated disease; complicated or high-risk cases need different management.

questions.question: A client passes large amounts of red blood per rectum and becomes hypotensive. What source should remain in the differential?
choices: A brisk upper GI bleed as well as a lower GI source
Only a hemorrhoid because blood is red
Only ulcerative colitis without further assessment
No bleeding because the stool is not black
questions.explanation: Hemodynamically significant hematochezia can arise from rapid upper GI bleeding. Resuscitation and source assessment must not assume a lower source from color alone.

questions.question: For ongoing hemodynamically significant hematochezia after initial stabilization, which diagnostic approach may help localize active bleeding?
choices: CT angiography under the team's protocol
Unprepared urgent colonoscopy for every client regardless of stability
Ignoring blood pressure if the first hemoglobin is normal
Delaying all source assessment until symptoms recur
questions.explanation: The updated ACG guidance supports CT angiography for ongoing significant bleeding; it can guide further intervention after resuscitation.

questions.question: A client with presumed IBD flare has new frequent bloody diarrhea. Which nursing action is important before assuming inflammation is the only cause?
choices: Support ordered testing for infectious causes and assess hydration and severity
Start an antimotility medicine independently
Dismiss fever as normal for every flare
Avoid documenting stool frequency
questions.explanation: Infection can mimic or complicate IBD activity, and severe colitis needs objective stool, vital-sign, hydration, and laboratory assessment.

questions.question: Which trend best supports recovery from a conservatively managed bowel obstruction?
choices: Decreasing pain and distension, improving hydration, and return of bowel function without new peritoneal signs
New rigidity and rising heart rate
Increasing NG output with falling urine output
Persistent vomiting despite worsening hypotension
questions.explanation: Resolution requires improving symptoms and fluid status with return of function; new peritoneal or perfusion abnormalities require immediate reassessment.
